list.listitem: Suspect Henoch-Schonlein purpura (HSP) in children with palpable purpura and abdominal pain, joint pain, proteinuria, or hematuria. B
Routine evaluation should include vital signs, CBC, urinalysis, and stool for occult blood; consider abdominal ultrasound if pain is severe or intussusception is suspected. C
Treatment is primarily supportive; acetaminophen as the preferred pain reliever. C
Prednisone should be used selectively in patients with more severe arthralgias or abdominal pain. B
Refer patients with severe abdominal pain, orchitis, or significant nephropathy. C

Henoch-Schonlein purpura (HSP) is an acute IgA-mediated leukocytoclastic vasculitis. Patients typically present with palpable purpura, abdominal pain, and arthritis. It is most common in children under the age of 10 years. While renal involvement is common, most patients recover uneventfully.
Incidence of hospitalization for HSP in Scotland: 20 to 27 per 100,000 children per year.
Incidence of HSP in a population of 155,000 children was 13.5/100,000/year.
It may be somewhat less common in the summer, although data are limited.

In HSP, IgA immune complexes accumulate in small blood vessels. This leads to the characteristic palpable purpura and also petechiae. When occurring in blood vessels of the kidney, they can cause glomerulonephritis, and when occurring in the GI tract, they can lead to bleeding.

A variety of common infections have been observed to precede the onset of HSP, including group A strep, parvovirus B19, helicobacter, coxsackie virus, and adenovirus. It is thought that exposure to these antigens may trigger the immune response that leads to HSP.
IgA vasculitis has also been reported following COVID-19 vaccination.

A meta-analysis of four clinical trials of patients with HSP, as well as a Cochrane review, concluded that corticosteroids, antiplatelets, and immunomodulating therapies (eg, cyclophosphamide, cyclosporine) made no difference in the likelihood of developing renal disease. B
Suspect HSP in children with palpable purpura and abdominal pain, joint pain, proteinuria, or hematuria. B
Routine evaluation should include vital signs, CBC, urinalysis, and stool for occult blood. C
In patients with more severe abdominal pain, consider ultrasound to exclude intussusception and other intraabdominal pathology. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Previous fractures and injuries, bruising of predominantly upper limbs, hand-print bruises, other signs of abuse.
Fever, arthralgias, family history, and chest or abdominal pain
Fatigue, fever, anorexia, diffuse bone tenderness; hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy.
Neurologic disturbances, signs of hemolysis, nausea or vomiting.
Nuchal rigidity, fever, petechial rash, mental status change.
Erythema or desquamation of palms and soles; bilateral conjunctival injection; cervical lymphadenopathy; fever; cardiovascular changes.
Fatigue, myalgias, intermittent spiking fever, headache, GI symptoms, history of tick bite.

list.listitem: The EULAR/PRINTO/PRES (2010) criteria for diagnosis of HSP were proposed by a consensus conference. They require the presence of purpura or petechiae with lower limb predominance, accompanied by at least one of the following: abdominal pain, abnormal biopsy showing IgA deposition, arthritis or arthralgias, or evidence of renal involvement (hematuria (>5 RBC/HPF, RBC casts or ≥2+ RBC by dipstick) or proteinuria (>0.3 g/24 h or >30 mmol/mg Urine albumin/Cr ratio on first morning urine).

American College of Rheumatology Criteria (1990) for HSP include the following four criteria: Age ≤20 years at disease onset Palpable purpura Acute abdominal pain Biopsy showing granulocytes in the walls of small arterioles or venules
Using a definition of two or more criteria as diagnostic for HSP is 87% sensitive and 88% specific (LR+ 7.2, LR− 0.15).
An ACR classification and regression tree algorithm had similar accuracy.

Suspect HSP in children with palpable purpura or petechiae, especially if they are palpable and predominantly in the lower extremities. Measure and monitor blood pressure during their illness as renal complications are relatively common.

A preceding respiratory infection was reported in 34% of adults and 21% of children with HSP. Elevated CRP and serum creatinine, hypertension, renal involvement, hematuria, proteinuria, and renal insufficiency were more common in adults than in children.

The EULAR/PRINTO/PRES criteria require the presence of purpura or petechiae with lower limb predominance, accompanied by at least one of the following: abdominal pain, abnormal biopsy showing IgA deposition, arthritis or arthralgias, and evidence of renal involvement (hematuria or proteinuria). These criteria were reported to be 100% sensitive and 87% specific in children, with an AUC of 0.93.
In a study of 350 adults, the EULAR/PRINTO/PRES criteria were 99% sensitive and 86% specific in adults. They were more accurate than the older ACR criteria.

Regarding individual elements of the definition, histopathology was present in 93%, arthritis in 78%, abdominal pain in 61%, and hematuria or proteinuria in 33%. Histopathology was the most specific single finding (91%).

In a study of 142 children and adolescents with HSP, about half had evidence of nephritis. The sole independent predictor of nephritis was the presence of severe abdominal pain (OR 2.6; 95% CI, 1.2–5.5). Another analysis in 134 patients found that in addition to severe abdominal symptoms, age >4 years and persistent purpura increased the risk of renal involvement and significant proteinuria.
Order a CBC with platelets to evaluate for possible anemia and thrombocytopenia, urinalysis to evaluate for hematuria, and PT/aPTT to evaluate for bleeding disorders.
Consider skin biopsy and IgA levels if HSP is suspected to confirm the diagnosis.
A skin biopsy can confirm the presence of leukocytoclastic vasculitis, and is part of the diagnostic criteria (although not required for diagnosis).

Patients with significant abdominal pain should have an evaluation to exclude intussusception, as well as appendicitis and other alternate causes for their symptoms. This may include, if necessary, abdominal ultrasound. Also evaluate the stool for occult or gross bleeding, which is common with HSP.

A study of 28 adults with HSP found that a positive test for antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) was 32% and 100% specific for HSP, and was associated with a greater likelihood of renal impairment. However, the small sample and case-control design limit the study’s conclusions.
A urinary monocyte chemotactic protein-1 (MCP-1) level above 530 pg/ml predicted a greater likelihood of nephritis in a study of 57 children with HSP.
A higher ratio of neutrophils to lymphocytes is associated with a greater likelihood of GI bleeding in adults with HSP, with a ratio greater than 3.2 being the optimal cutoff (LR+ 3, LR− 0.33).

A clinical decision rule was developed to predict the likelihood of “severe gastrointestinal involvement” defined as abdominal pain accompanied by gross blood in the stool. Predictors included elevated WBC count, elevated d-dimer, lower Factor XIII levels, serum sodium <136 mEq/L, and serum albumin <3.8 g/dl. However, the sample size was small (only 11/113 with the outcome of interest) and it has not been prospectively validated.

Suspect HSP in any patient with purpura or petechiae in the lower extremities, and in those patients ask about abdominal pain and joint pain, and obtain a urinalysis. This will usually allow you to make the diagnosis if one of these three clinical characteristics is present in addition to purpura or petechiae.
Consider skin biopsy to confirm the diagnosis in the absence of other symptoms, and check the stool for occult blood.
Treatment is primarily supportive; acetaminophen is the preferred pain reliever. C
Prednisone should be selectively in patients with more severe arthralgias and abdominal pain. B
Strongly consider referring patients to the appropriate specialist if there is severe abdominal pain, orchitis, or evidence of nephrotic syndrome or nephritis. C

Treatment of HSP is primarily supportive, as the vast majority of patients recover without sequelae. Acetaminophen is recommended for joint and abdominal pain. While NSAIDs are an option, they should be considered second-line and should be avoided in patients with evidence of GI bleeding or renal involvement.

The use of corticosteroids is somewhat controversial. Studies are few and of mixed quality, with significant heterogeneity with regard to dose, duration of treatment, and timing of initiation. Prednisone 1 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks (initiated within 7 days of onset), and then weaned over the next 2 weeks, was shown in an RCT of 171 patients to reduce the severity of abdominal pain and joint pain more than placebo, and to reduce its duration by about a day. It should be considered for patients with more severe abdominal or joint pain, but not used routinely for all patients.

A randomized trial compared prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day (maximum 80 mg/day) with placebo in 352 children with HSP. The drug was started within 7 days of the onset of purpura. There was no significant difference in the likelihood of proteinuria (15% taking prednisolone, 10% taking placebo).

A systematic review of four studies concluded that neither prednisolone nor cyclophosphamide reduced the likelihood of renal complications in children with HSP. Similarly, a Cochrane review concluded that neither prednisolone (5 studies, 746 children, RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.42-1.32), heparin (2 studies), nor antiplatelet agents (3 studies) reduced the likelihood of persistent kidney disease. A long-term follow-up of patients in an RCT of prednisone found no long-term benefit in terms of renal function.

A Cochrane review identified 9 studies of interventions in patients with severe IgA vasculitits associated kidney disease, including mycophenolate mofetil, corticosteroids, and heparin. While one study with 228 children found that heparin reduced the likelihood of renal involvement at 3 months, the authors conclude that it is not warranted given the potential adverse effects and the rarity of serious renal disease.
Refer to the 2022 KDIGO guidelines for the management of glomerular disease for patients with renal complications.
A case report described the successful treatment of bullous lesions with IV immunoglobulin after steroid failure.
Patients with significant proteinuria or casts in the urine should be referred to a nephrologist.
Boys with scrotal pain or swelling should be evaluated by a urologist for possible orchitis.

A prospective study of 223 children found that 46% developed evidence of nephritis, 9% nephrotic proteinuria, 0.5% nephrotic-nephritic syndrome, 22% have fecal occult blood, and 14% of boys have orchitis.
About 1 in 7 boys experiences orchitis, and testicular torsion is a possible complication. When clinically suspected, patients should be evaluated by a urologist.
Intussusception is a rare complication (<3%) and requires urgent surgical referral.
While hematuria and proteinuria are common, permanent impairment of renal function is rare. B
Recurrence is relatively common, especially in older children and those with renal involvement. B
Risk factors for renal involvement included older age, male sex, abdominal pain or GI bleeding, severe bowel angina, purpura, relapse, and thrombocytosis. B .

A prospective study of 223 children with HSP found that 46% developed evidence of nephritis. Of the 102 with nephritis, 14% developed isolated hematuria, 9% isolated proteinuria, 56% both, 20% nephrotic proteinuria, and 1% nephrotic-nephritic syndrome. The average onset was at 2 weeks, and only 2% developed it beyond 2 months after onset. The same study found that orchitis occurred in 14% of boys, and 22% of patients tested had fecal occult blood.

A prospective study followed 270 children with HSP over a 13-year period (mean 8.3 years of follow-up). Only 20% (55) had any initial evidence of renal involvement. All 37 (67%) children with isolated hematuria or hematuria with mild proteinuria recovered completely. Of the other 33% (18), 1 died acutely and only 3 had any persistent urinary abnormality, none of whom had an elevated serum creatinine or major histologic changes.

In a systematic review of 12 studies with 1,133 children, permanent renal impairment occurred in no patient with a normal urinalysis, in 1.6% with isolated urinary abnormalities (proteinuria or hematuria without nephritic or nephrotic syndrome) and in 20% who were diagnosed with nephrotic or nephritic syndrome.

A meta-analysis of 9 studies identified older age at onset, lower glomerular filtration rate, initial renal manifestations with nephrotic syndrome, with nephritic-nephrotic syndrome and renal biopsy with crescentic nephritis were associated with a higher risk of poor renal outcomes.
Recurrence is relatively common, occurring in up to one-third of children.

A prospective observational study followed 78 persons with HSP nephritis in childhood for a mean of 23 years. They found that 44% with a nephrotic or nephritic syndrome had hypertension or impaired renal function, compared with 18% who presented with hematuria.
Risk factors for renal involvement included older age, male sex, abdominal pain or GI bleeding, severe bowel angina, purpura, relapse, and thrombocytosis.

A retrospective study of 57 adults with HSP found that about half had renal involvement, including 23% with biopsy confirmed IgA glomerulonephritis. Predictors of glomerulonephritis included preceding infection, fever, and purpura present above the waist.

An observational study of 202 adults with IgA vasculitis found that end-stage kidney disease was more likely in older patients (24% compared with 14% of middle-aged and 3% of younger adults). Risk factor for ESKD included diabetes, black race, male gender, and GFR < 30 ml/minute at presentation.
A higher ratio of neutrophils to lymphocytes is associated with a greater likelihood of GI bleeding in adults with HSP, with a ratio greater than 3.2 being the optimal cutoff (LR+ 3, LR− 0.33).

In a study of 58 children with HSP, age less than 9 years, low-grade proteinuria, and a rapid (<2 week) onset of renal abnormalities was associated with a shorter duration of renal abnormalities. Children with abdominal pain, those who experience a recurrence of HSP, and those older than 8 years were more likely to develop nephritis.
Monitor blood pressure and urinalysis regularly for 6 months. If normal at that time, significant renal disease is extremely unlikely.
